desc:
A positive integer is deci-binary if every digit in its decimal form is 0 or 1 and it has no leading zeros. For example 101 and 1100 are deci-binary, while 112 and 3001 are not.

The positive integer n is given as a string of digits. Return the minimum number of deci-binary numbers that add up to n. The same number may be used more than once.

n = "32"    -> 3   (10 + 11 + 11)
n = "82734" -> 8
n = "111"   -> 1
constraints: n consists of digits only, has no leading zeros and is greater than 0
hints: Look at a single column of digits. One deci-binary number can contribute at most 1 to that column.
If some column holds the digit 7, how many addends are needed just to produce that column?
The answer cannot be smaller than the largest digit of n, and it is always possible to reach that bound. Return the largest digit.
editorial: Every deci-binary addend adds either 0 or 1 to each digit position, and there are no carries to worry about as long as the total of a column is at most 9. A column that must reach the digit d therefore needs at least d addends, so the answer is at least the maximum digit m of n.

That bound is achievable: build m addends, and in each column of digit d put a 1 in exactly d of them (any d of the m). Each addend then has digits 0 and 1 only, and none is zero because the column holding the digit m gives a 1 to every addend (leading zeros of an addend simply make it a shorter number). So the answer is just the largest digit, found in one pass.
